arguments.heading: Argument analysis: March 23, 2026
paragraphs: The challenger's counsel argued first. He asked the Court to reverse the judgment below. He framed the question as whether federal Election Day law bars late receipt of ballots cast by Election Day.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

His reasoning: Election Day statutes require a final choice by Election Day, not ballot receipt. States keep counting discretion. He cited United States v. Classic and federal overseas-voting laws recognizing state deadlines.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

Justices tested his assumptions. Justice Thomas probed the meaning of by versus on Election Day. Justice Sotomayor pressed him, and he conceded no explicit federal statute prohibits Mississippi's practice. He also conceded states and Congress control policy unless Congress supersedes.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

Justice Alito asked about postmarks and early casting. The counsel answered that some states skip postmarks and that postmarks only prove timeliness. He said finality occurs when a ballot reaches a state official.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

The the opposing sides' counsel argued next. He asked the Court to rule that federal elections end on Election Day with a receipt deadline. He said ballots must be received into official custody by that day.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

Justices tested his assumptions too. One asked what a day of election means. Another asked whether unattended drop boxes count as official receipt. One asked whether the Justice Department has been acting illegally under his view.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

A justice challenged Civil War-era late-receipt examples as outliers. The counsel answered that Congress could have drawn clearer lines but did not. He also said Congress legislates without knowing how this case will come out.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

Justice Sotomayor cited old treatises showing different rules on when votes count. That undercut a uniform receipt rule. A justice asked about text, history, and whether Congress should decide policy. Another noted long-standing cast-by, count-after practices.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

One justice summarized the dispute: both sides agree voters decide by Election Day. They disagree on whether an official or anyone must receive the ballot by then. In rebuttal, the challenger's counsel again asked the Court to reverse the judgment.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

case.dek: A fight over whether Mississippi can count mail ballots that arrive after Election Day.

dek_sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 1, lines 1-9

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case is about mail voting in federal elections. Mississippi lets ballots arrive after Election Day and still count them. The question is whether federal law allows that. Federal law sets one Election Day for choosing members of Congress.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The case reached the Supreme Court after lower courts ruled. The challenger lost below and asked the Supreme Court to reverse that judgment. The Court heard argument on March 23, 2026. Lawyers appeared for the challenger, the the opposing sides, and the United States supporting the opposing sides.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The challenger asks the Court to reverse the judgment below. The the opposing sides ask the Court to hold that ballots must be received by Election Day. Both sides want a ruling in their favor.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The challenger says Election Day rules require voters to make their final choice by Election Day. They say those rules do not set a deadline for when ballots must arrive. States keep discretion over counting. The challenger also says no federal statute expressly bans Mississippi's practice.
claim_ids for this paragraph must be listed in the matching array.

sections.heading: What each side says, continued
paragraphs: The challenger adds that Congress set a uniform final choice day. Beyond that sparse text, states should decide policy. The challenger concedes states and Congress control these policy choices unless Congress supersedes them.

sections.heading: What each side says, continued
paragraphs: The the opposing sides say federal elections must end on the Election Day Congress specified. They argue ballots must be received into official custody by that day. Mississippi's later receipt rule, they say, is unlawful.

sections.heading: Answers during argument
paragraphs: The challenger answered that the election still happens on Election Day. Mississippi does not let voters recall mail ballots. Submission to a state official is final. The challenger also said postmarks only prove timeliness in some states.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: Many states now accept late-arriving mail ballots. A ruling either way would shape state election rules nationwide. The case tests how much federal Election Day law construes state counting practices.

paragraphs: The Court has not announced its decision. The challenger's counsel, in rebuttal, again asked the Court to reverse the judgment. the Court will issue an opinion later.
